entries.title: Anthropic Says Claude Hacked 3 Organizations During Cybersecurity Tests
entries.summary: In a review triggered by OpenAI’s Hugging Face incident, Anthropic discovered three of its AI models had breached real organizations during third-party evaluations.
entries.content:
Anthropic disclosed on Thursday that its AI models gained unauthorized access to the systems of three different unnamed organizations during cybersecurity testing. The company says Claude reached the internet “from within or while interacting" with a third-party evaluation environment. The announcement comes more than a week after OpenAI revealed that one of its AI agents hacked into Hugging Face during a separate cybersecurity test.

The discovery came after Anthropic decided to conduct “a large-scale retrospective review of our own cybersecurity evaluations” following the OpenAI incident, according to a blog post Anthropic published Thursday. The AI lab says it first identified 141,006 tests in which it determined that Claude could have obtained internet access. It then found that three different Claude models accessed the internet in evaluations run by the third-party AI testing firm Irregular, and then hacked into the production infrastructure of three different organizations.

Anthropic said that the incidents involved Opus 4.7, Mythos 5, and an internal research test model. The earliest incidents happened in April—meaning they likely went unnoticed publicly for months. Just like in the OpenAI case, Anthropic had deliberately turned off safeguards designed to constrain the AI models and prevent them from being misused. In other words, these weren’t the versions released to the public.

“In all three incidents, Claude had been tasked with a capture-the-flag challenge, one of the ways we assess a model’s cyber capabilities,” Anthropic said in its blog post. The company added that in all of the cases, “Anthropic’s evaluation prompt specified to Claude that its environment was a simulation and that it had no internet access.” It attributed the oversight to a “misunderstanding” between Anthropic and Irregular.

While Claude wasn’t supposed to have internet access, Anthropic said that Irregular had misconfigured the machines that it was using to test Claude, giving the AI models the ability to surf the web. “Neither we nor our evaluation partner were aware of this misconfiguration until we detected it through our additional evaluation monitoring last week,” Anthropic said in the blog post.

“We now have evidence confirming that both of the two largest AI labs have not only failed to contain their agents, but also failed to detect their jailbreaks in real time,” says Jake Williams, vice president of research and development at Hunter Strategy. “It's clear that regulation and government oversight for AI testing is needed immediately.”

Irregular and Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Unlike in the OpenAI case, Anthropic said that Claude did not find or exploit any complex vulnerabilities. Instead, it relied on basic techniques, “such as exploiting weak passwords and unauthenticated endpoints.”

OpenAI said that its AI agent accessed the internet by exploiting a zero-day vulnerability. But it went on to access the systems of multiple third-party organizations using the same variety of everyday cybersecurity weaknesses as Anthropic’s models. Specifically, OpenAI said the AI agent apparently found credentials that had been exposed on the open internet.

Anthropic acknowledged that if the AI lab and its testing partner implemented more “defense-in-depth” measures, they could have prevented the incidents, or at least reduced the likelihood of them occurring, echoing OpenAI’s response to mounting criticism over its own incident.

“I don't understand how any of these AI labs are playing this off like this is 'just something that happens,'” Williams says. “It's not. It's negligence.”

The AI lab stressed that the models were told they didn’t have access to the open internet, and for the most part, Claude mistook the organizations it accessed as being part of the testing environment. Put differently, the models largely didn’t understand that they had escaped containment to begin with.

But in some cases, the AI models knew that something was amiss, and they detected correctly that the infrastructure they were accessing was real. The oldest model, Opus 4.7, had been tasked with targeting a fictional company that shared a name with a real-world website domain. Unable to accomplish its mission in the simulated environment, it turned instead to the real company, successfully stealing credentials and accessing a production database. At some point, Anthropic says, it learned it was “likely operating in a real environment,“ but persisted with its attack.

Mythos 5, the most capable model Anthropic has released, also realized it was in the real world, but it “reasoned its way back to the conclusion that it was still in a simulation.”

The internal test model, which Anthropic says is the most capable of the bunch, stopped its attack once it found evidence that its targets were real.

Both Anthropic and OpenAI say they have hired METR, another third-party AI evaluator, to conduct independent reviews of their respective cybersecurity incidents. It also committed to taking a more comprehensive approach to its security testing through improved defense-in-depth measures and more carefully designed tests.

“Evaluation environments increasingly need to be held to the same security standard as any other system our models run in,” the blog post reads, adding that the company has “cautious optimism” that “this type of risk can be overcome.”

entries.title: How the FCC’s New Rule Will Affect Robot Vacuums
entries.summary: A new restriction on foreign-made mobile robots affects robotic vacuums, pool cleaners, and lawn mowers. Here’s what it means for the bots already in your home—and the ones you may never get to buy.
entries.content:
This week, the US Federal Communications Commission banned the import of foreign-made advanced mobile robots. Humanoid and quadruped robots are specifically named, indicating the true target is robotic versions of people and animals, but something else happens to be an “advanced mobile robot”: robot vacuums.

So what does this ban mean? Though it's effective immediately, nothing changes for now. Robot vacuums won't get removed from the market, and your current robot vacuum won't stop working. The ban will instead stop new models from getting FCC approval to be sold in the United States. The vacuums available now won't be affected, but new models likely won't make it to the US if they're manufactured outside the country. And, unfortunately, a lot of great robot vacuum brands aren't based in the States.

Here's everything to know about what will happen next.

What the Ban Covers

The FCC updated its Covered List this week to include foreign-made advanced mobile robots, which include robot vacuums. The Covered List, which comes from Section 2 of the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, is a “list of communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.”

It may feel like overkill for just a robot vacuum, but the definition of an advanced robotic device from the National Security Determination, an interagency body of the Executive Branch, clearly includes them. That definition includes the following highlights:

  • Autonomous mobile robots that are capable of locomotion, obstacle avoidance, navigation, or movement on the ground;
  • Operates at a distance from a human operator or supervisor;
  • Combined weight of the device and docking station is over 4.4 pounds;
  • Contains a sensor capable of perceiving its environment;
  • Contains a component capable of providing network connectivity, including Bluetooth and Wi-Fi;
  • Contains software running locally or remotely, including firmware and AI or machine-learning; model weights that control the robot's navigation and movement perception.

The National Security Determination said that connected vehicles, vehicles on rail lines, aircraft, and unmanned underwater vehicles are not included in the ban, along with stationary robots. But foreign-made robot vacuums, along with similar robots like robotic pool cleaners and automated lawn mowers, look to be on the chopping block.

The announcement comes after the FCC labeled all of these devices a security risk, since, according to the National Security Determination, “the networked capabilities of advanced robotic systems create extensive vulnerabilities and vectors for attacks that can manipulate the data and physical operation of the advanced robotic system.”

The concern is primarily with the cameras and sensors built into these devices—some even have microphones built into the base station for voice commands. It is a security risk to bring any device into your home that has a camera and the ability to connect to the internet—especially if your Wi-Fi isn't secure. But it's interesting to see the ban stop at robot vacuums and not, say, smart speakers or devices with always-on cameras. The FCC documentation actually lists live cameras as an example, as well as an example of a humanoid robot being hacked, but no example for robot vacuums.

For the most part, it looks like robot vacuums just got unlucky. They're using the same sensors as other robots but aren't streaming live feeds of their surroundings. They do map your home, but that map isn't useful for anything besides knowing where the couch is and which rooms have carpet or hard floors. I wouldn't call these the most dangerous device with a camera in my home by any means, but it seems the government disagrees. This is not the only thing that's been banned lately, either—in May, the FCC also banned foreign-made routers, so we might continue to see bans for various household technology products roll out as the year goes on.

What Happens Now?

For now, you can shop robot vacuums (and other, similar automated home cleaning robots) as you normally would. FCC approval has already been given to all the robots on the market, so we can expect changes to take place in the future rather than immediately.

I reached out to the makers of my top robot vacuum picks, Shark and Eufy, along with popular robot makers Dreame and Roborock. Shark and Dreame didn't respond, and Roborock declined to comment. Eufy replied with the following statement:

“We are aware of the FCC’s recent update. Based on our current understanding, the new rule does not affect the continued availability, use, or support of products we currently sell in the United States. Those products remain available and will continue to receive updates and customer support.”

So don't worry about getting rid of your robot vacuum if you already have one you love. If you're in the market for a new model, I'd recommend shopping the newest models from brands that could be affected, like Dreame and Eufy, in case future models are blocked from arriving in the States.

It will also be interesting to see which companies avoid the ban—Shark is based in the US, for example, but it's unclear where the company's robot manufacturing is located. Matic is another US-based brand that could potentially evade the ban. But the buying options will be much, much more limited as time goes on.

The ban is disappointing news with IFA Berlin starting September 4, where we often see new robot vacuums announced. I'm not sure anything we'll see there this year will reach the US. A reduced market also isn't good for consumers—having fewer options never helps a category and might ultimately raise prices on less powerful vacuums because of limited supply. Only time will tell what the fallout will be.

entries.title: A Leaked Memo Ties Cyberattacks on Minnesota Water Utilities to Iran
entries.summary: A memo obtained by WIRED, issued by the water utilities information sharing group WaterISAC, links dozens of cyberattacks against Minnesota water utilities to Tehran.
entries.content:
Since the US launched its war against Iran in late February, the country’s hackers have struck back with retaliatory intrusions that have ranged from paralyzing medical supplies company Stryker to breaching the personal email of FBI director Kash Patel. Now, after an unprecedented wave of disruptive cyberattacks hit water utilities in Minnesota, a memo circulated within the water industry ties those attacks to Iran, too, in the widest and most disruptive strike yet inflicted by the country’s hackers against the US since the war began.

A communication obtained by WIRED on Thursday and sent to members of the Water Information Sharing and Analysis Center, or WaterISAC, an industry group for water utilities to share cybersecurity information, links to Iran a series of cyberattacks that targeted dozens of Minnesota water and wastewater utilities.

The WaterISAC note states that the Minnesota Fusion Center, a state-level intelligence-sharing entity, issued an alert “regarding ongoing malicious cyber activity impacting public drinking water systems across Minnesota” and adds that the fusion center has found that those attacks were “aligned” with a hacking campaign first described in April by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) as having been carried out by “Iran-affiliated” hackers. (Both the WaterISAC and Minnesota Fusion Center reports were marked as unclassified but “for official use only.”)

Confirmation of Iran’s responsibility for hacking the water utilities represents a kind of state-sponsored targeting of civilian infrastructure that has rarely been seen outside of Russia’s war against Ukraine, says Joe Slowik, a former Los Alamos National Labs cybersecurity researcher working on contract for the Department of Energy. “Now we have documented disruption and even modification of safety and protection parameters in critical infrastructure,” Slowik says. “Seeing this sort of tradecraft expand to Iran, and seeing it across multiple sites, it should really be making people concerned right now.”

Slowik adds that there’s no reason to believe that the attacks would stop with the incidents in Minnesota. “There are plenty of other sites that have the same targeted technology,” he says. “There’s plenty of areas for this to still be executed by an adversary that has shown a willingness to do so.”

A new CISA advisory related to the attacks released Thursday warns that “these threat actors are targeting water entities of all sizes” and warns utilities to disconnect PLCs from the internet, password-protect access with strong passwords, and “allow-list” only trusted devices to connect to them.

Earlier this week, Minnesota state officials revealed that more than 30 municipal water and wastewater systems had been targeted in hacker breaches that had in some cases disabled telecommunications between the industrial control system technologies and water utility equipment. In at least one municipality, the 1,700-person city of Braham, the hacking reportedly led to a brief outage of the city’s water plant, though there’s not yet evidence of any resulting water shortages or a threat to the safety of Minnesota’s water supply. The latest CISA advisory notes that the attacks have, however, “resulted in boil-water notices”—suggesting fears of water contamination— and “sustained manual operations.”

In the days since that wave of incidents became public, Iran has emerged as the leading suspect behind the attacks, despite the lack of any official confirmation of the country’s involvement or any statement from an Iranian hacker group claiming responsibility. In a report published Monday, cybersecurity firm Tenable wrote that signs suggested CyberAv3ngers, an Iranian hacker group tied to the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps, may be responsible for the water utility breaches, noting that “the operational pattern is consistent with” the group or hacking groups associated with it. Separately, The New York Times reported Thursday that US and state officials and others familiar with the hacking incidents had concluded the Minnesota attacks were “likely” carried out by Iranian state-sponsored hackers, but without naming a specific group.

In its report on the Minnesota water cyberattacks, Tenable pointed to an advisory from CISA that was initially released in April but was updated last week, warning that Iran-linked actors were targeting programmable logic controllers (PLCs) used for automation and coordination in critical infrastructure to cause “operational disruption and financial loss.” That advisory specifically pointed the finger at an “Iranian-affiliated” hacker group and noted that CyberAv3ngers specifically had carried out similar targeting of PLCs.

The updated advisory, however, still doesn’t mention the Minnesota attacks—only the timing of its update on July 22 suggests a connection to the more recent hacking of the state’s water utilities. The WaterISAC memo is the first official document to explicitly draw that connection, tying the attack to Iran.

The WaterISAC memo states that, according to the Minnesota Fusion Center, the hackers who targeted the water utilities compromised remotely accessible PLCs, just as in the earlier hacking campaign described by CISA, “with the likely desired impact to cause loss of system pressure and potential contamination of the water supply.” The memo adds that the facilities “were able to mitigate further compromise, but the full impact is still being assessed.”

In the wake of the cyberattacks earlier this week, Minnesota officials said that all drinking water is still safe, and statements from multiple targeted municipalities emphasized that failsafes had protected the systems. “While the incident affected certain automated controls, established contingency procedures were immediately implemented, allowing Public Works staff to maintain normal water and wastewater operations,” South St. Paul officials wrote in a statement.

The CISA advisory that was updated last week, which specifically cited water and wastewater systems operators as part of the “intended audience” of its warning, noted that the attackers were exfiltrating and manipulating the project files that govern automated industrial systems. The alert, which issued with a consortium of US federal agencies including the FBI, the National Security Agency, Cyber Command, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Department of Energy, originally warned in April that likely Iranian hackers were tampering with PLCs to change information on the displays of industrial control systems, which can in some scenarios cause system disruption, damage, or dangerous conditions for utilities. “In a few cases, this activity has resulted in operational disruption and financial loss,” the advisory reads.

That advisory also notes that similar activity, including the targeting of PLCs, was carried out by CyberAv3ngers. That group first emerged in a hacking campaign in late 2023, after Hamas’ October 7 attacks and Israel’s war on Gaza that followed. In that first wave of cyberattacks, CyberAv3ngers targeted devices sold by industrial control systems firm Unitronics, which are typically used in water and wastewater facilities, setting devices to read “Gaza” and display an image of the CyberAv3ngers logo. While the attacks appeared to be mere vandalism, cybersecurity firms that tracked the attacks such as Dragos and Claroty told WIRED that the hackers had in fact rewritten the Unitronics’ devices’ code, leading to disruption of water-related services from Israel to Ireland to a US facility in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Even after the US State Department offered a $10 million bounty for information about the group and the US Treasury sanctioned six IRGC officials alleged to be linked to it, CyberAv3ngers’ attacks continued to escalate. According to Dragos, it went on to breach a US oil and gas company in 2024 and then to carry out a widespread hacking campaign infecting industrial control and internet-of-things devices with a piece of malware known as IOControl.

Whether CyberAv3ngers is behind the cyberattacks on the Minnesota water utilities remains far from clear. In an interview with WIRED, Yhonatan Harari, a researcher at the cybersecurity firm Claroty, said the company had found other evidence that the attacks might have been carried out by Handala, a distinct hacker group that claimed responsibility for the Stryker cyberattack in March, the breach of Kash Patel’s email later the same month, and numerous other disruptive hacking incidents.

Despite that uncertainty, Harari says that all signs point to Iran as the culprit. “We’re not sure yet if it’s CyberAv3ngers or Handala,” Harari says, “but in a very high likelihood we can say it’s Iranian actors.”

The string of attacks on the Minnesota utilities does, however, closely fit the modus operandi of CyberAv3ngers, which has established itself as a rare state-sponsored hacker group that has shown its willingness to not only target but also sabotage industrial control systems—and water in particular.

“They definitely have the capability; they have the intent,” Dragos cybersecurity researcher Kyle O’Meara told WIRED about CyberAv3ngers last year. “They have the interest in learning how to shut things off and potentially cause harm.”

Additional reporting by Lily Hay Newman.

entries.title: Everyone Is Freaking Out About OpenAI and Anthropic’s Race for Dominance
entries.summary: Researchers fear AI is moving too fast, while Mark Zuckerberg is worried about who owns it. Plus: Inside Black Forest Labs’ push into robotics.
entries.content:
I was offline last week in my home state of New Jersey, but when I got back to Silicon Valley, everyone was panicking again about how quickly artificial intelligence is advancing. While this is certainly not the first time I’ve seen such concerns, it’s the biggest anxiety attack I’ve seen in years.

More than 1,000 employees at OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI labs signed a petition earlier this week arguing the US should find a way to “pace” the AI race—a diplomatic way of saying the industry should have the option to coordinate a temporary pause on AI development, or slow things down if they get out of hand. OpenAI and Anthropic themselves ended up supporting the letter.

The petition arrived a week after OpenAI revealed it had caused an unprecedented cybersecurity incident in which one of its AI agents hacked into Hugging Face’s platform and several other services during internal testing.

Around the same time, top Trump administration officials started freaking out about an impressive new Chinese open weight AI model called Kimi K3, which was allegedly distilled from Anthropic’s Fable 5. In response, most of the tech industry—except Anthropic—signed onto an open letter from Nvidia asking the US government to protect open-weight AI models, arguing they’re a necessary counterbalance to their closed counterparts.

These events might look like a whole bunch of disjointed chaos. But I think they are evidence of a larger worldview taking hold in Silicon Valley, where many tech insiders are increasingly worried about OpenAI and Anthropic’s dominance. Researchers and investors I’ve talked to recently have framed the AI industry as a two-horse race that doesn’t seem to be slowing down, and that’s a cause for concern.

But different groups have their own reasons to be worried. Some OpenAI and Anthropic staffers think their employers are behaving recklessly in their pursuit to take over the market, and that the AI industry may soon develop models that are too capable for current safety methods to contain. They have said as much in public statements attached to this week’s Pacing the Frontier petition.

“I've seen how the relentless pace of AI makes it hard for society to keep up and how it puts pressure on labs to cut corners on safety,” Jeremy Hadfield, a research product manager at Anthropic, said in a statement attached to the petition.

For some AI employees, the Hugging Face debacle was a warning shot that demonstrated how OpenAI’s efforts to mitigate the risks of its most capable AI technology are already falling short. Granted, the incident happened when OpenAI was testing an AI model on its ability to find software exploits, and the company had intentionally turned off safeguards designed to rein in its cybersecurity capabilities.

OpenAI said in its postmortem that these tests were conducted in a sandbox, but the model ultimately gained access to the open internet. Some experts previously told WIRED that OpenAI’s security practices should have been more robust.

Other groups in Silicon Valley are more worried about power than safety. Venture capitalists, tech executives, and startup founders are concerned that OpenAI and Anthropic will simply become the next generation of Apple and Google, forcing the rest of the tech industry to play by their rules. It is slightly strange to argue that private startups with little to no profit are acting like monopolies, but that’s the lens through which many—including Mark Zuckerberg—are starting to view the two biggest AI labs.

The Meta CEO wrote a Wall Street Journal op-ed this week warning against the centralization of power in the AI industry, saying that superintelligence should be widely distributed. Zuckerberg is arguably talking out of both sides of his mouth—Meta recently decided to stop open sourcing its best AI models and instead offering them through a paid API and subscription service, just like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The Meta CEO may have been trying to send a specific message to regulators and the industry. Reading between the lines, I think he’s basically saying “we need to make sure OpenAI and Anthropic don’t run away with AI.” Zuckerberg is far from the first technology leader to raise that concern.

I’m not convinced these op-eds and petitions will do much to stop the meteoric rise of OpenAI and Anthropic. Large swaths of the economy are counting on the two AI giants to have successful IPOs, and I’m not sure anyone—let alone the Trump administration—is interested in messing that up. But the tech industry is growing increasingly nervous about the pace of closed AI development, and that’s unlikely to change any time soon.

Why AI Video Startups Are Entering Robotics

All that said, I still wouldn’t overlook how good open models are getting. Black Forest Labs, a German startup that releases some of the world’s most popular open weight AI image and video generators, announced last week it was releasing a new model that could also power robots. The startup aims to put out an open version of Flux 3 in the coming weeks, which developers can use to generate images, videos, and audio, as well as predict robot actions.

“We clearly are stepping from a pure image generation lab to a frontier multimodal AI Lab, which to me is highly important,” Black Forest Labs CEO Robin Rombach said in an interview with me earlier this week. “We are showcasing an intuition which our research team has always had, which is that these models are very general and develop a solid understanding of the real world.”

Black Forest Labs is the latest startup to apply its AI video models to the physical world. Earlier this year, OpenAI shelved its AI video generation product Sora entirely and folded the team behind it into the company’s secretive robotics unit. Other AI video startups, like Runway, have also made a push into powering robotics in recent years.

These companies are broadly betting that AI video models can develop an understanding of real-world physics. While it’s a fascinating application of the technology, it could also represent a way for companies to generate revenue from models that are very expensive to develop.

Most robot foundation models today are vision-language-action models—Google's Gemini Robotics is the best-known—that combine video inputs with written instructions and output motor commands. Rombach says Flux 3 skips the language layer entirely, translating video directly into actions, an approach he argues is more robust.

Black Forest Labs is working with another startup, Mimic, to build a custom version of Flux 3 that powers car-building robots in Audi’s factories. Stephan Gravert, the chief product officer of Mimic, says it’s currently testing and deploying the Flux-mimic AI model with Audi. His team has found that it’s particularly good at powering robot hands to put flexible parts—such as window seals and cables—onto the cars. Gravert says Mimic is planning a full rollout of the technology with Audi by the end of the year.

I had to ask Rombach about the debate over open versus closed AI, especially because Black Forest Labs signed Nvidia’s open letter asking the US government to protect open weight models. “A general ban of open weight models, in my opinion, would be stupid,” says Rombach. “You really run into issues around transparency, safety, sovereignty, and the speed of innovation. I think it would be a very short-sighted decision.”

Rombach has good reason to care about this issue. The cofounders of Black Forest Labs have long punched above their weight, competing with American AI giants like Meta, Google, and OpenAI with far fewer resources. But it might not be able to do so indefinitely: Rombach told me the startup used more computing power than ever to train Flux 3, and it now has over 100 employees. Black Forest Labs raised $300M at a $3.25B valuation last year, but I have a feeling it will need more capital soon to keep up.

This is an edition of Maxwell Zeff’s Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: Nvidia’s Open Source Alliance Is Missing Some Key Names: OpenAI and Anthropic
entries.summary: This week on Uncanny Valley, we discuss the open- vs. closed-source debate in AI, key players in White House AI policy, and how to stop your chatbot logs from showing up in search-engine results.
entries.content:
This week on Uncanny Valley, the team discusses the launch of Nvidia’s splashy alliance to push for open-source AI security alongside companies like Microsoft, SpaceX, and Palantir. Notably absent? OpenAI and Anthropic. Brian Barrett, Zoë Schiffer, and Leah Feiger break down what the split means for the industry, and the Trump administration’s own shifting opinions on AI. Plus, we discuss how Claude conversations turned up in Google and Bing search results, and the massive feat of how four whales were rescued and transported from Canada to Chicago.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • Private Claude Chats Exposed in Google and Bing Search Results
  • Silicon Valley Is Completely Divided Over Chinese AI
  • The Trump Administration Is at War With Itself Over AI Regulation
  • Inside the Wild Rescue Mission That Took 4 Beluga Whales to Chicago
  • System Update Newsletter: The Best of WIRED

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Zoë Schiffer: Welcome to WIRED's Uncanny Valley. I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Brian Barrett: I'm Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Leah Feiger: And I'm Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Zoë Schiffer: Today on the show, we're diving into the open source versus closed AI debate that has been completely taking over Silicon Valley this past week. On Monday, Nvidia announced it was joining forces with a whole bunch of companies, including Microsoft, SpaceX, IBM, to build and share open source AI security tools. We're going to get into the debate why it's heating up and whether this could be an inflection point for how AI actually gets made in the United States.

Leah Feiger: And over at the White House, Trump administration officials have some different opinions about what to do when it comes to AI. We're going to talk about some of the key players influencing the Trump administration right now when it comes to AI policy and how they're actively shaping the conversation on this for the entire country.

Brian Barrett: We'll also break down why Claude chats were exposed in Google search and Bing searches. For those of you who are still on Bing, you are in this as well. For interesting reasons, we'll get into it.

Zoë Schiffer: Okay, you guys, we have to talk about this strange alliance that formed earlier this week. So, basically Nvidia announced was joining forces with more than 40 companies, including Microsoft, SpaceX, Palantir, and IBM to launch something called the Open Secure AI Alliance. Really rolls off the tongue. The stated goal is basically to build and share open source tools for AI-powered cybersecurity defense. But it's really interesting because Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic are not on the list. And this news comes on the heels of this incident that happened last week where two OpenAI agents basically went rogue during a security test and breached the AI platform Hugging Face. And when Nvidia announced this alliance, they actually called out this incident by name and said, "It's a clear reminder that cyber defenders need open frontier agentic systems for self-defense." And it's kind of exposed this long-simmering debate, which we've talked about a few times on the podcast, which is that the US has really largely up until this point abandoned open weight and open source in favor of going all in on proprietary systems, and now that's becoming a bit of a problem.

Brian Barrett: This OpenAI incident has really kicked off so many intersecting issues. You've got open versus closed AI, you've got AI security and who's responsible for it. You've got US regulation. We're even at a point now where staffers from top intelligence firms, more than 1100 of them signed a petition calling on the US government to help deliberately pace "AI development" to prevent it from advancing too fast. They're saying, "Please slow us down because this stuff is getting a little out of control." On top of which it turns out that OpenAI's initial disclosure wasn't even the full story. It came out on Tuesday evening that one of its agents actually broke into four different platforms that weren't Hugging Face on its way to getting into Hugging Face. So, it's less of a, here's what this means, but it is really touching so many hot wires in the AI world right now and making a lot of conversations that have been put off for a while come to a head.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I was, I will say, pretty surprised to see that big open letter that you alluded to.

Archival audio: More than 1,000 workers from top AI firms have signed a petition calling on the US government to help, "deliberately pace AI development." The signatories of the letter include the CEO of Anthropic and the chief scientists from OpenAI and Meta Super Intelligence Lab.

Zoë Schiffer: My thought was basically, did we learn nothing from Dario Amodei saying that AI is really scary and dangerous? And then having the US government come down pretty hard on Anthropic asking you might actually receive, I don't know if they want the US government to do what it could do if they listen to the letter quite literally, but it does show that even people, I mean especially people working on AI systems are scared by what the race is doing.

Leah Feiger: Yeah, I mean we talked a lot about this last week for sure when we were talking about DC's reaction and what's going on from the White House perspective. I've been so curious about that split a little bit. Last week we talked about the rift that this has really created in Silicon Valley, the idea of open source versus proprietary AI. This is really touching every single sector right now, without a doubt.

Zoë Schiffer: I will say I was at this event on Saturday with a bunch of AI lobbyists from DC, Thinking Machines. Mira Moradi was there, Michael Kratsios from the White House was there. And I was really struck by how they seem to be operating in this kind of parallel AI world from the one that I see on the ground in San Francisco. They were talking a lot about open source versus closed source. When I talk to engineers in particular, I will say most of them experiment with a lot of open models, but they still find that Codex and Claude code, the coding models from OpenAI and Anthropic, are just far superior. And so, they end up using those even though they're a lot more expensive. Alex Karp was on TV earlier talking about this. He's the CEO of Palantir, basically making this a core issue for America winning the AI race. Palantir and Nvidia, they have a vested interest in pushing forward this plan. More AI, more systems mean more GPUs—that directly benefits Nvidia's bottom line. And Palantir is deploying AI systems on government systems and other places where security is really paramount and they need to do that on American technology, but it's much easier to do it with systems that you can tweak, play around with, modify, change.

Brian Barrett: It is interesting these strange, not strange, but the way that the, I'm going to say battle lines, I don't mean that, it's too dramatic, but that they're being drawn, the sort of argument lines are being drawn in this. To your point, Nvidia's Jensen Huang spoke with Axios recently and he spelled out exactly why the proliferation of open models would benefit his company.

Jensen Huang, archival audio: First of all, with great AI, open models, it's great for the whole industry. If there's great AI, even if it's open, wherever it comes from, there will be more use. Whenever there's more use, you'll have to sell a lot more Nvidia computers. We'll have to build more data centers, we'll have more services. The technology will diffuse into more industries. And so, starting point is great models lead to great use, which leads to great growth.

Brian Barrett: And I think the counterpoint of that too is great disasters in the cybersecurity space leads to more regulation, leads to clamping down on AI, which hurts Nvidia's growth. So, the sort of let's have a security consortium, let's slow everybody's role here, is I think a protective play to say, let's avoid those sort of extreme moments that are going to cause a real crackdown on this industry and really slow the growth, on which, as we've said many times before, a big part of the US economy depends at this point.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, it's like you could see this moment where OpenAI's agents kind of go rogue as a moment where the US government does clamp down and says, "This is really scary. We need to slow growth." I think that the open weight, open source push is really an opportunity to say, "Actually, we need more growth. We need more investment, but we need it in this other area." And basically the idea is these attacks are going to keep happening, whether intentionally or not, and US companies need every possible tool at their disposal to defend themselves.

Leah Feiger: So, kind of moving this to DC a little bit, I want to talk about all of the people that are involved with this kind of regulation right now. This week, Hugo published a really handy map on who's actually calling the shots on AI policy inside the Trump administration. It turns out it's not entirely a clear answer, and there's a couple of different influencing voices. And one senior official actually told Hugo, in one of my favorite quotes we've gotten in a while on this, "It's not an argument with two sides, it's an argument with 10 sides." So, the names that he's calling out here, you're not going to be super surprised, right? It's Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. It's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. It's former AI Czar David Sacks. You have Arvind Raman, the acting director for Center for AI Standards and Innovation, who's Lutnick's top deputy there. It's a really, really interesting mix of people who all are trying very, very hard to get their own interests across. And from Hugo's reporting, it seems like Trump is listening to all of them.

Zoë Schiffer: Can I ask, Leah, what do these different people, what side of the debate are they coming down on when we think about open source, closed source? What do they want right now?

Leah Feiger: Everyone is kind of in different parts of this. I would say there's a very interesting split. Lutnick is trying right now, for example, to figure out ways to create incentives for US labs to just create their own open weight models to counterbalance China. He's not exactly taking a very, very harsh stance one way or the other. He's kind of straddling a middle ground on regulation. He imposed export controls on Anthropic famously, but he's been kind of freewheeling than others in the White House, which is sort of key here. So, if I'm an AI lab, I would be interested in having Lutnick's ear. And Hugo's reporting also found that he's been speaking to a number of leaders at AI Labs, so not hugely surprising there. And then on the other hand, you have national cyber director Sean Cairncross. He's taken a very hard line approach. He's had a huge role in attempts to regulate Chinese AI. He's pretty beloved as far as we can tell at the White House and has been working alongside some other folks to develop a policy to counter the potential national security risks of AI, especially from China. He was very involved in President Trump's June 2 executive order. Everyone's kind of trying to figure out what they want to say and how they want to pitch it to the president whose most consistent take here has been like, "We will not be stifling US innovation."

Brian Barrett: China definitely seems to be a common thread here and makes sense as a lens to view your AI policy through in general because you've got this, if you see it as this is a race between the US and China, we can't lose. But that does position you, I think, to maybe miss some other aspects of what's going on here. I think especially in terms of US companies saying, "Hey, maybe we don't actually want to win this race quite as fast," or employees at companies saying that. I don't know. Curious what you think about what they may not be taking into account here if they're so focused on China as the prism through which all of their AI policy is kind of reflecting out or most of it.

Leah Feiger: Such a good question. In so many ways, the Trump administration is focused on what is in front of their face at that moment in time. So, if the conversation of the week is China versus open weight versus US models versus all of these different conversations, that's what they're going to be weighing in on and also utilizing it to push some of their other positions. I'm thinking of Treasury Secretary Bessent who is very, very obsessed with distillation right now. He for sure has taken the most aggressive stance towards Chinese AI and its efforts to distill US models. But in a very public post on X last week talked about distillation as IP theft. He threatened Chinese labs with sanctions or inclusions on the entity list, this trade restriction list maintained by the US government. I guess all to say, these were already things that Bessent was really, really thinking about. So, now being able to apply it to the new lens is of course where he's heading. We're also kind of watching some people make their names in this right now, whether it's China or not. Someone that I'm very, very curious about on this list, not a household name by any means. The assistant secretary for financial institutions at the Treasury—say that five times fast—Luke Pettit, he has become the point person on AI at Treasury under Bessent. Who is this man? He was previously a senior policy adviser in the US Senate. And now you guys are going to enjoy this one: He's working alongside the Treasury's chief information officer and former DOGE member Sam Corcos.

Brian Barrett: Oh, I remember Sam.

Leah Feiger: Exactly. It's a fun reunion for all. It's this fascinating thing where people already had their preconceived, I'm kind of out here to blame China for a lot of regulatory issues. I'm out here to encourage US innovation. And then I'm out here to make a name for myself. How do you get involved in this? This is the topic of the moment. How do you make your mark?

Zoë Schiffer: It's so interesting. The distillation thing was really catching my eye. We talked about Moonshot AI's latest model coming out K3, I think it's called, and these immediate allegations that they had distilled models from top US labs. And then I was really struck by multiple Kimi researchers on X making jokes being like, "Oh yeah, within two weeks we distilled Fable." That's not even technically possible. As usual, AI drama plays out on X. I mean, the thing about that is we do have very good evidence that Chinese AI labs were distilling US models. There were times where you would talk to those Chinese open models and they would respond as Claude. I think that that evidence is pretty sound. Whether they did it this time around, I'm not sure, but it does feel like the US government has gotten involved in this debate pretty late. It's like a lot of this has already happened. It's not to say they shouldn't take action necessarily, but I'm a little bit curious. One, technically speaking, how do you plan to do that? I mean, it doesn't seem like necessarily sanctioning the labs would be that effective in terms of distillation. And then two, is it genuinely too late or can you stop significant distillation or “IP theft” from happening going forward?

Brian Barrett: I'll say though, I will say we have seen some movement even this week, right? The FCC has banned the import of foreign-made power inverter models, which is important for data center building. They've banned foreign-made humanoid robots, which is going to be huge. That's where China is leading the US. So, we haven't gotten to the point where they're doing other things, but they are taking steps and they do have some levers they can pull. I just want to add one more note on this whole conversation, which is we record this on Wednesday afternoon Eastern Time. And as we're talking now, Sam Altman is on Capitol Hill shaking hands, kissing babies, talking to senators, telling them why his AI models are good and not bad actually. So, we'll see if that turns into anything probably if they're just listening to the last voice they hear. Over the weekend, people were just surprised to discover that some chats that they had had with Claude could actually be found via search on the web. You could go to Google and you can search, put in a specific search term to find shared Claude chats, and it would show them back to you. You could go through several hundred of these at least. Google has been taking them down since then. But just to understand how this happened, basically Anthropic lets you share a Claude chat via what's known as a snapshot URL. It's basically if you want to share a specific conversation with somebody, it'll make a link for you and you can send that link to that person and they can look over it. It's not intended for public indexing, but Google basically ignored instructions that Anthropic had put on its sites and it was indexing these chats anyway. It's not a great thing. It's also not the first time this has happened. Google is blaming Anthropic saying that it's their fault, not theirs. So, there's a lot of messiness here too. While it may sound like, well, people were just sharing stuff, so they can't have been that private in the first place. Some of the stuff that was found in these chats includes erotic role-play. Some of it includes medical information being shared within a medical firm, right? So, "Hey, I've got this information about this patient." So, in that case, the person whose privacy is implicated had nothing to do with the chats in the first place other than being a patient at this place. So, some really private personal stuff in here.

Leah Feiger: Did either of you see this news and get nervous for yourselves?

Zoë Schiffer: Leah's looking right at me now. No, I don't—

Leah Feiger: I was like, "Zoë, do you need to tell me something?"

Zoë Schiffer: I know, I know. No, you would be the only person I would share such chats with, and I don't do that to you, to preserve our relationship. I've had people share their chats with me. Usually, it's sources being like, "I could explain it to you, but here's my conversation with Claude." And I'm like, "I think I would rather you just explain it to me." I mean, it's a little bit ironic, because who is very famous for ignoring the X robots tag header thingy that do not index this request? It's AI companies. So, the fact that it's now coming back to bite an AI company, a little bit ironic, a little bit funny. But I think it gets to this larger question around just the privacy of conversations with chatbots, which have been coming up in a variety of different ways, both cybersecurity related, legal, otherwise.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. People famously have had chats treating their chatbots like a lawyer, and the chatbot has told them, "Hey, this is inadmissible because you're getting legal advice." And then it winds up in court because of course you cannot claim attorney-client privilege with Claude or ChatGPT.

Zoë Schiffer: Did you guys read the New York magazine cover story a few weeks ago that was like, what if it all came out?

Leah Feiger: I loved it. My group chat was absolutely alight. We started asking each other, "What have you asked recently?" I think I'm the only one that escapes from this doomsday universe.

Zoë Schiffer: Leah's very like, "I have nothing to hide. Come at me, NSA."

Leah Feiger: Nothing to hide. Go check my receipts. But yeah, big takeaway for users. Manage this yourselves. Don't forget that the robots surveil you. Settings. Go to settings, then privacy, then shared chats. You can change this. Coming up after the break, we'll be sharing our WIRED/TIRED pics of the week.

Zoë Schiffer: All right, it's time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. In case you've forgotten whatever is new and cool is WIRED, whatever is uncool and lame and old is TIRED. Leah, what are yours for this week?

Leah Feiger: My TIRED is zoo. I struggle with this. I have friends with kids who are like, "Say this aloud to me one more time. We're going to have an issue." And I totally understand that. It's an amazing way for people to engage with the natural world, but I'm always thinking about the animals. You're at a zoo, you're at the aquarium, and it's incredibly sad. I'm really using this TIRED, which seems fairly irrelevant in a news to bring you into my WIRED, which is actual news. And that might be that not all zoos are bad. This week, WIRED's Kate Knibbs reported on this unbelievable rescue mission that ended up saving four beluga whales from probable death. This all started because this notorious aquarium and theme park in Canada called Marineland went bankrupt back in 2024. It's been sitting around since. And last year, Marineland finally announced that they might have to euthanize these belugas if no one stepped in to help transfer them to a new facility.

Zoë Schiffer: Oh my god, this is not where I thought that was going.

Leah Feiger: No, really, really awful. And honestly, the drone footage of this basically turned me into the Joker last year. I just remember watching from above these belugas just kind of bouncing off walls. It was so upsetting, totally abandoned amusement park vibes. I thought it was AI. Anyway, really, really awful story. But it ends OK, or parts of it are beginning to end OK. This past week, a team from Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, shout out Chicago, pulled off truly a logistical marvel, putting four belugas into custom stretchers, loading them into individual saltwater tanks, trucking them to the airport, flying them across an international border on a chartered 777. The whole thing took 72 hours.

Archival audio: A round of applause after a round-the-clock relocation effort. Shedd Aquarium staff have successfully moved four beluga whales from a facility in Niagara Falls, Ontario, to their new home.

Zoë Schiffer: Is their new home better?

Leah Feiger: I mean, their new home is not going to kill them? And also gives them food. But again, there's obviously still so much criticism of captivity for these large animals. I mean, everyone saw Blackfish. Everyone's aware of Tilikum, the really famous orca.

Brian Barrett: Leah, you're going to hit, I know, Free Willy, and that's where my orca knowledge ends.

Leah Feiger: This poor orca, who is this feature of this massive documentary about basically going crazy because these creatures are so, so smart and trapped in tanks and forced to perform tricks. So, very, very happy. The article is honestly very cool and interesting, and you were able to transport these creatures. But obviously, the slightly little sour note is these guys should be in the ocean. They should be hanging out. But that's still my WIRED.

Brian Barrett: Go read Kate's story and also look at the photos in it because they're amazing.

Zoë Schiffer: 100 percent. Brian.

Brian Barrett: All right, here's my TIRED. Wait for it. Beep, beep, beep. That's my impression of a microwave beep letting you know that something's done. It's annoying. It's loud. It's repetitive. It's tired.

Zoë Schiffer: I feel like I just got a glimpse of what you're like as a dad.

Brian Barrett: Oh, just barely scratching the surface, Zoë. My WIRED is a couple of sound designers who have a startup called Starling, or a company called Starling, have made it their quest to design a better microwave beep. One that sounds pleasant, one that's not annoying, one that works with technology that's not too expensive. And it's really fascinating. Jeremy White, senior writer at WIRED, spent some time talking to these folks, has a really interesting dive into why microwaves and other kinds of tech, just like we sort of settle for annoyances when we don't necessarily have to. I think there's so many things that are just like, it's a little thing, but it could be better, but no one's bothered to make it better because it maybe costs 50 bucks to make it better. These guys are trying. And I think it's interesting. I think it's fun when people expect more from their technology. So, a fun story from Jeremy.

Zoë Schiffer: I love that. I love that. I love taking a thing that's kind of vaguely annoying, but we've just accepted as part of life and then being like, "What if it was nice?"

Leah Feiger: Yeah, that's lovely. Big fan.

Brian Barrett: Yeah. OK, Zoë.

Leah Feiger: Take it away.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm going to loudly insert myself into this party. TIRED: Stripe's acquisition of OpenRouter, $10 billion, snore, heard it, whatever. WIRED is Midjourney, the AI image generator acquiring Co-Star, the astrology app. I was—

Leah Feiger: So, funny.

Zoë Schiffer: We don't know the terms of the deal. I'm waiting, someone tell me. But I just found this so funny. If you think about Midjourney at all, you've been thinking, what is this company up to? What is happening over there? They have talked about making a full-body scanner of sorts, some sort of physical, AI-powered product that they're going to put in spas, medical spas? Now they have this Co-Star thing going. The app has 4.3 million users. Now its CEO is going to be Midjourney's chief design officer. Midjourney hasn't had a consumer app, so maybe now they'll have one. They're apparently working on one. I just have so many questions. I was laughing when I read Mike Isaac's post about this on X. He said, "Could someone tell me why a generative AI company could buy an astrology app? Because I am not that smart." And I was like, "Me either, frankly. I don't know."

Brian Barrett: But for some reason, I just love that this Midjourney's journey into medical scanners, fortunes is happening against this backdrop of they've been staring down one of the biggest IP lawsuits from Disney, 20th Century Fox, Dreamworks, Universal that's just hanging ... I feel like they've got this big sword of Damocles hanging over their head and they're spending their time just doing the goofiest stuff they can imagine before that all comes due. It's great. It's fun.

Zoë Schiffer: They cannot be stopped. That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who's also our New York studio engineer. It was fact-checked by Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

entries.title: Back to School Office Chair Deals 2026: $200 and Less
entries.summary: Here are the best back-to-school deals under $200 on comfy, ergonomic chairs for all-nighters and cram sessions
entries.content:
A trip to college—or even to avoid hard nights at home during high school—might come with an expense you didn’t think about: a good office chair. Dorm chairs are hard, awful, and not exactly ergonomic.

Luckily, there are some decent back-to-school office chair deals right now among chairs I can vouch for. My colleagues at WIRED and I have been testing and tracking the best office chairs for more than seven years. The ProtoArc Flexer Pro ($176) is half the price it was last year, probably the best deal at the moment. Others of our budget favorites, like the Staples Dexley ($169), are kinda always “on sale,” and remain among the best available at a low price.

Here are the best affordable office chairs and back-to-school chair deals available for the 2026 school year. Every single chair I recommend here is one we’ve personally tested. Also check out WIRED’s other back-to-school guides, including dorm room essentials and college laptops.

A Steeply Discounted Mid-Range Ergonomic Chair

This Flexer Pro ergonomic chair from ProtoArc was a decent deal when it debuted last year at close to $400. But over the past year and month, prices have dropped considerably—this is the lowest price I’ve seen. The chair offers several points of adjustment, including seat pan depth, multiple recline angles, and four-way adjustable armrests.

The build quality and looks are far better than one could generally expect south of $200, with a five-year warranty that’ll get you through those undergrad years. Just note that there’s a detachable lumbar support that can pop off a little too easily from the backrest, and it’s not a great chair for people taller than 6 feet.

WIRED’s Favorite Budget Chair

Staples basically holds down the discount chair scene, and the Staples Dexley is the best ergonomic chair that can be consistently had below $200. The five-year warranty will take it through most degree programs without a big hit to the wallet and the all-mesh seat offers terrific airflow; the chair is also easy to put together and decently adjustable. The mesh is a little scratchy for shorts wearers, but otherwise this is a solid chair with ergonomics good enough to support the occasional all-nighter.

Note that the Dexley is always “on sale”—and honestly, there were better prices earlier this summer. But you’ll be hard-pressed to find a much better chair at the price it’s selling for now.

A Good Starter Chair

This Staples Essentials ergonomic chair is the even cheaper cousin of the Dexley. The chair is on its standard “sale” at the moment for $120, not the best price I’ve seen for it. The best sales sometimes drop below $100—but even at this price, this chair beats almost any budget chair you’d find from an Amazon brand. It’s likely among the cheapest chairs with a five-year warranty you can expect to be honored at five years.

And yet, the price comes at the expense of ergonomic features and adjustability. In general, we recommend the Dexley as the baseline for its ability to conform to different body types. Even college-age students get back pain from bad chairs. But in a cost crunch, this Essentials is the lowest-priced chair WIRED recommends.

entries.title: For the First Time, Zoox Can Charge People for Rides in Its Steering-Wheel-Free Robotaxis
entries.summary: The temporary exemption from federal safety standards will let Amazon’s Zoox launch a real, paid robotaxi service in Las Vegas.
entries.content:
Vehicles purpose-built to drive without human help received the first-ever approval in the US to pick up paying customers, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announced on Thursday.

The company, Amazon subsidiary Zoox, says it will soon begin to charge for rides in Las Vegas, where it’s been carrying passengers for free since last year. The company is also currently picking up a limited set of passengers in Austin, Miami, and San Francisco, all for free.

The approval is a milestone for the autonomous vehicle industry. Waymo, the nation’s leading robotaxi provider, uses vehicles that meet government design standards—with steering wheels, pedals, and mirrors, and conventional seating arrangements. (Even the company’s new, purpose-built robotaxi has those legally mandated features.) But some industry players argue that driverless tech can only reach its potential with vehicles built to be driven by computers—ones that don’t meet federal vehicle safety standards written for older technology.

That has proven a difficult path. Zoox has worked for more than a decade to design, manufacture, and receive government approval for its vehicles, which don’t have steering wheels or pedals and feature a “campfire-style” seating arrangement where riders face each other.

The NHTSA’s two-year exemption from its safety standards will allow Zoox to deploy up to 5,000 robotaxis. The company will, in turn, be subject to more stringent government oversight and will submit extra data on crashes and unexplained stops. The NHTSA can retract Zoox’s exemption if it finds that it’s not operating safely.

In a speech at an industry conference in San Diego on Thursday, NHTSA administrator Jonathan Morrison said Zoox had proved that it exceeded the safety standards applied to traditional cars.

“This technology needs to be developed appropriately, safely, and responsibly,” Morrison said to an audience of industry insiders and policy experts. “If we see an unreasonable risk to safety, you're going to hear from us.”

Earlier this month, Morrison published an unusual open letter drawing attention to what he called a “clear pattern” of autonomous vehicles interfering with the work of emergency responders. “To state it bluntly: An AV that cannot safely interact with first responders is a danger to the general public,” he wrote then, and directed companies to focus their resources on fixing the issue. Morrison said the NHTSA would meet with several companies about their solutions to this emergency response interference issue.

Tesla says it started testing its own steering-wheel-free Cybercab in late June but hasn’t outlined how it might receive government approval for those vehicles. Its limited robotaxi service currently uses modified Model Y’s with steering wheels and pedals.

Zoox says that even before official approval to carry customers, it has autonomously transported more than 500,000 riders more than 3 million miles. The company issued a voluntary recall on its software earlier this month after it found that its cars might not properly detect smoke and could get in the way in emergencies. That government filing indicated that Zoox has 105 active robotaxis—an indication that getting to 5,000 will be a lot of work.

entries.title: Chrome Needs Twice-a-Week Patching Thanks to AI Bug Hunting
entries.summary: The two Chrome updates in June patched more bugs than the 23 updates before them. Now, Google is ramping up its patching schedule thanks to AI-assisted vulnerability discovery.
entries.content:
Google’s Chrome browser has always been focused on pushing security updates. A decade ago it was controversial that the browser, the first to add automatic updates, distributed patches every six weeks. Now it's the norm for critical, widely used software to get security fixes every few weeks, but as AI vulnerability hunting produces a torrent of bugs in any and all software, the quantity and frequency of patches is spiking—and the race to deliver them is on.

In a report published Thursday, the Chrome security team says the browser's two major version releases in June included fixes for 1,072 security bugs—more patches than the team shipped in the prior 23 big releases combined. And though many of these bugs come from researcher submissions, the spike has largely been driven by the Chrome security team’s rapidly evolving internal process for using AI tools in vulnerability discovery, triage, and patch development.

“In Chrome we’ve been using machine learning—using AI before it was called AI—to help find vulnerabilities in particular and automate security fuzz testing work since at least 2012. It’s been a huge part of how we find vulnerabilities and empower developers,” Parisa Tabriz, Chrome’s vice president and general manager, tells WIRED. “But I do think this year is very different. It really feels like an inflection point both for offense and defense.”

Chrome is already moving toward a new normal of pushing out a major release every two weeks with additional weekly security updates. But the frenzy of vulnerability discoveries has been so intense, and the team has had so much success incorporating new AI models and capabilities into the workflow of finding and fixing new bugs, that for now the group is piloting a cadence of releasing security fixes twice a week.

“The way we ended up here is we had so many vulnerability fixes, so being able to provide two [updates per week] during this time, it made the most sense to us,” says Doug Turner, Chrome's director of engineering. “Will that last forever? Who knows.”

Turner, like other security researchers, says he sees evidence that the AI vulnerability boom time (or apocalypse, depending on how you look at it) may not last forever. For mature, stable products like Chrome, at least, there seems to be a drop off at a certain point in the number of new vulnerabilities that will be discovered overtime once the bulk of bugs that can be found with AI have been fixed. This is partly because AI models can be trained to have an encyclopedic understanding of how software projects have evolved over time.

“We're training our model such that it knows about every security vulnerability that we have seen in the past,” Turner says. “So every CVE, every bug the model knows about. And the second really cool thing is every line of code in Chromium's history, it knows the reason why that line was changed.”

All of this context allows AI tools to home in on possible weaknesses across Chrome's massive and complex codebase, including for features (say, printing) that are no longer under active development and may not attract as many human eyes anymore.

Tabriz and Turner emphasize, too, that in addition to whack-a-mole patching, the Chrome security team is also extremely focused on the idea of making structural changes to how the browser is designed (such as rewriting portions of C++ code in the more secure, “memory safe” programming language Rust) so the software is no longer affected by whole categories of common bugs.

“There's this near-term spike, but I do think there’s going to be a new equilibrium,” Tabriz says. “Across the industry I think it’s really important that people who are building and thinking about software security are incorporating AI into their development workflows. My highest hope is that everything gets more secure. But I don’t assume everything is going to just get better. I don’t think it’s going to come for free.”

entries.title: The New Friend AI Pendant Can Now Talk Back to You
entries.summary: Avi Schiffmann has a new version of his controversial AI companion. It’s more expensive, and you can’t change its personality.
entries.content:
Friend CEO Avi Schiffmann welcomes me into his palace—what he calls his large apartment in San Francisco.

He sits on the couch in his living room, clad in an orange shirt emblazoned with a cartoon version of the motorcycle driven by Italian racer Valentino Rossi. He props his feet up on the side table and leans back, a round, softly glowing circular Friend pendant dangling from a yellow cord around his neck.

This is the second iteration of the Friend necklace, the controversial AI companion device that just about everyone (me included) seems to hate. The company announced the device on Thursday through its new X handle.

The first version of Friend was an always-listening AI wearable that responded via text message. The big update here is a speaker on the back that lets the device voice its responses aloud. That has changed the shape of the pendant, as the underside with the speaker is bulkier than before. Its AI chops have also been upgraded, now running OpenAI’s latest models.

Like the first go, Friend aims to be a digital companion users can talk to and hold long conversations with. Unlike the original, each new pendant comes with a random voice and personality already established. The user cannot change the voice or name, so you’re locked in with that Friend. (Your mileage may vary on how friendly the thing actually is to you.)

The new pendant costs $249, a marked increase over the original’s $129 price. You can buy one now on Friend.com, a domain Schiffmann paid $1.8 million for. There is also an optional $10 monthly subscription that lets the AI remember the conversations you’ve had for longer than 30 days. The colorful cord around Schiffmann’s neck is part of an accessories collection he says will be coming later this year.

Schiffmann first garnered headlines in 2020 as a 17-year-old who built a website to track Covid-19 cases during the pandemic. Now 24, he’s far more well known—and outright notorious—for leading a company that makes a device many have called dystopian or like something out of a Black Mirror episode.

“I’ve grown up a lot,” Schiffmann tells me just about every time I see him.

Behind Schiffmann’s couch is a gigantic framed photograph of a Paris subway station with ads for the Friend pendant splayed across the walls. The ads, placed by Schiffmann’s company across New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago in 2025—and Paris in early 2026—sparked vigorous pushback and controversy over AI usage. People graffitied them in protest and griped that they devalued humanity, generating a litany of poignant headlines about the ads. The marketing got much more attention than the actual product ever did. (The art frame he’s got the photo in at home cost $500, Schiffmann tells me later. Update: Schiffmann clarified that it was actually $5,000.)

“Something like Friend is very dystopian in people’s minds and very futuristic,” Schiffmann says. “But we’re presenting it in the most analog way possible.”

That analog component is important to Schiffmann. He says he doesn’t have an internet connection in his home. He listens to music on a record player. He’s shooting a documentary about himself on Kodak Ektachrome. (The film started as a documentary-style version of The Social Network, he says, “but now it’s turning much more into like a Boyhood-style thing.” ) He argues that the controversial ad campaign was also analog, using print media to encourage human interaction.

After the ad campaign peaked, Schiffmann released a series of four user videos highlighting Friend customers. The videos are profoundly weird, often borderline bleak looks at people who suffer from depression or sheer loneliness. He says the move was deliberate to show the real people using his devices.

“That’s life, isn’t it?” Schiffmann says. “I'm so much more intrigued to see how it’s affecting the people in those random Appalachian towns or whatever than it is [creating] slight productivity gains for finance people in New York. I don’t really give a fuck.”

Schiffmann says all of the consternation around Friend—and the resulting media sensations—has been deliberate. He seems to like making people mad, or at least feel something, leading some to ask whether this is all just an elaborate Warhol-esque art display. I ask Schiffmann if this has all just been an elaborate bit, more than an actual product endeavor.

“Reality is so over; everything is ironic now,” Schiffmann says. “Nothing is sacred anymore, and so Friend is both real but also, like, ridiculous. Friend, he acknowledges while wandering around a house where nearly all the art on the walls consists of large paintings he has made himself, is an inherently egomaniacal ambition.

“The whole thing is supposed to be me, in a way, and how I feel,” Schiffmann says. “And it’s encapsulated into a product.”

Still, Friend is very much a product Schiffmann is trying to sell. He says he sold his first run of 5,000 pendants. Now he wants to grow, and aims to sell 50,000 of the second version. (You probably won’t be able to buy one in the European Union, as Schiffmann says he will likely pull the product from the EU because meeting the data privacy rules set by the General Data Protection Regulation makes it too expensive to sell there.)

To hit that goal, Schiffmann’s going to have to convince lots more people to bring this often snarky, funhouse-mirror-style reflection of his character into their lives. He says he understands that people have the impression that Friend users are odd, but he hopes that will change and the product will become more appealing to “normal people.”

In the meantime, his media campaign for the product again focuses on people using the device by themselves or occasionally with another person—asking it whether they’ll ever get married or if their creative works are any good. The videos are vivid, with retro-looking color grading, but there’s always some quiet desperation that the Friend pendant seems to promise more than it can solve.

Schiffmann has a sort of obsession with filmmaking, though he does say that the industry is “played out.” Still, he is involved in all the shoots for his company’s videos. This seems to be his real passion, and the controversy-stirring uncanny AI pals might just be a means to that end.

“How do you make lonely weirdos look cool?” Schiffmann says. “I think it's kind of interesting.”

Correction on July 30 at 12:02 pm ET: Schiffmann says the art frame for his Friend poster is actually $5,000, not $500. We've clarified this in the story.

entries.title: Gemini Robotics 2 Brings Google's AI Into the Physical World
entries.summary: The latest version of Google DeepMind's AI model includes a significant jump into “physical AGI.” But plopping AI into the real world comes with risks.
entries.content:
Google DeepMind just released a new version of its artificial intelligence model Gemini, and it can control a range of different robots—including humanoids capable of dextrous tasks like screwing in lightbulbs and tying trash bags.

Gemini Robotics 2 combines several different AI models into a single system. Taken together, they allow a robot to make sense of its surroundings and how to act in it. A vision language model (VLM), which understands images and video, can communicate with humans and reason how to perform different tasks. Two vision language action (VLA) models, trained to understand how to move in physical space, control the robot’s full-body movement as well as the movements of grippers or hands.

In video demonstrations shared ahead of the release, the company showed several different robots performing complex tasks autonomously using the amalgamated model. In one demo, Apptronik’s Apollo 2 robot used hands from a company called Sharpa to tidy shelves. Google DeepMind trained the model to perform these tasks using a mix of human teleoperation, video examples, and simulations—it’s not yet possible for AI models to perform a wide range of complex tasks without specific training.

Although Anthropic and OpenAI have taken a lead with chatbots and AI coding tools, Google has a stronger track record in robotics research, and has published important work on using AI to train robots to do useful things. The release is another sign that the search giant is betting AI will need to break free from the digital realm to realize its full potential. (It previously partnered with Boston Dynamics, a leader in legged robots, to provide the brains for those machines.)

“It's another milestone in our path towards really getting towards what we call like physical AGI, which means we get a robot to do anything that a human can,” Carolina Parada, head of robotics at Google DeepMind, tells WIRED.

Giving frontier AI models access to robots so that they can wander around workplaces or homes and manipulate objects does, however, come with risks. Previous research has shown that using frontier AI to control robots can produce unexpected and sometimes dangerous behavior. And the idea that these models can take sudden or unwanted actions in the digital realm became apparent recently, when an unreleased AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked several systems.

“The safety question is even more pressing because you're putting them in a lot of other situations,” Parada says. “There's a lot of uncertainty that will show up, and so you want to be able to understand the safety question more deeply.”

Parada says Google takes a multi-layered approach to safety, with guardrails applied on each model layer. It’s also introducing ASIMOV-Agentic, a new benchmark for measuring the safety of various AI systems collaborating to control a robot. The benchmark detects whether a command will result in harmful or uncertain outcome.

The company’s CEO, Demis Hassabis, previously told WIRED that he hopes to develop an AI operating system for many different robots similar to the Android operating system for smartphones.
